etymology: From the Greek Kürillos (“lordly,” “masterful”), a diminutive of kürios, “lord.” He is styled “of Alexandria” from the great Egyptian see he held (c. 412–444), successor to his uncle Theophilus.
biblical_def: Cyril of Alexandria stands among the foremost defenders of the true doctrine of the Person of Christ, that in the incarnate Lord there is not a mere conjunction of two loosely-joined persons but one Person, the eternal Son, who took our nature into union with Himself. When Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, shrank from confessing that the One born of the virgin was very God, refusing her the title Theotokos (God-bearer) rightly understood as safeguarding the deity of her Son, Cyril contended against him and prevailed at the Council of Ephesus in 431. That the child in the manger was no other than the Word made flesh, John 1:14, that He who suffered was the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:8 — this Cyril laboured to establish, and the church confessed it after him at Chalcedon. His writings upon the unity of Christ’s Person, and upon the Gospel of John, remain a rich mine of Christological truth. Yet the same hand that guarded the deity of Christ also pressed the honour of His mother beyond what Scripture warrants, sowing seed that would ripen into the Marian corruptions of Rome; and his patriarchate was stained by the factional violence of Alexandria. We honour his Christ, and we mark his errors, that we may hold the one and refuse the other.
webster_summary: Fifth-century patriarch of Alexandria who defended the unity of Christ’s Person against Nestorius at Ephesus, though marred by Marian excess and factional violence.
webster_full: CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA, proper noun. A bishop of the Egyptian church, patriarch of Alexandria from about 412 to 444.
The principal opponent of Nestorius and champion of the one Person of the incarnate Son at the Council of Ephesus, 431.
Author of extensive commentaries, especially upon the Gospel of John, and of dogmatic treatises on the unity of Christ.
A teacher whose Christology the church received, yet whose devotion to the virgin outran Scripture and prepared Marian error.
A patriarch whose administration was disfigured by the factional and mob violence of his city.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high.
corruption_summary: A defender of Christ’s Person whose later Marian excess and factional violence must be named plainly as error.
corruption_paragraphs: Cyril’s labour for the unity of Christ’s Person is honourable and true, and the church rightly received it. But his exaltation of the virgin, though it began as a guard upon the deity of her Son, was pressed beyond the warrant of Scripture, feeding a devotion to Mary that Rome would afterward inflate into invocation, mediation, and immaculate conception — corruptions that rob the one Mediator, Christ Jesus, of His sole glory, 1 Timothy 2:5. This is not a difference of emphasis to be smoothed over; it is error, and the Reformation’s recovery of Christ as the alone Advocate was recovery from precisely such corruption.

His patriarchate, further, was marked by the factional and mob violence of Alexandria, a zeal that ran to the shedding of blood and the crushing of rivals rather than the meekness of wisdom that is from above, James 3:17. Faithfulness to the truth of Christ never sanctifies the works of the flesh in its defence; the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, 2 Timothy 2:24. We hold his Christology and we reject both his Mariology and his violence, honouring what is honourable and naming error error.
roots_summary: That the child of the manger is very God, one Person, the Word made flesh — and that no defender is above correction.
roots_lines: The one born of the virgin is the eternal Son, God of God, who took our nature into personal union with Himself.
He who suffered upon the cross was the Lord of glory; the fulness of the Godhead dwelt in Him bodily.
To guard the deity of Christ is honourable; to exalt His mother beyond Scripture is corruption, however it begins.
The truth of Christ is never advanced by the violence of the flesh, for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
We may honour a teacher’s doctrine and refuse his errors, proving all things and holding fast that which is good.
usage: Cyril’s stand at Ephesus secured the confession that the One born of Mary is very God.
The Reformation recovered Christ as the sole Mediator from the Marian excess that Cyril’s devotion helped to seed.
We honour Cyril’s Christology while naming his factional violence and Mariology as error, not tradition.

etymology: From the Greek Hippōlutos, “loosed horse” or “unyoked steed” (from hippos, horse, and lúō, to loose), a name borne in Greek legend and afterward by this Christian writer of the Roman church (c. 170–235).
biblical_def: Hippolytus of Rome was among the most learned Christian writers of the early third century, a disciple in the line of Irenaeus, prolific in commentary and controversy, who laboured against the heresies of his day and left an exposition of Daniel and of the Song of Songs, along with a great refutation of the errors that troubled the church. His learning was real and his zeal for sound doctrine against Gnostic and Modalist corruptions was commendable, so that the church has profited from what he wrote in defence of the truth. Yet his story is a solemn warning, for this same man, in his contention against the bishops of Rome whom he judged too lax toward penitent sinners, withdrew from the communion of the church and set himself up as a rival bishop, so that he is reckoned the first of the antipopes. His rigorism — a severity that would shut the door of restoration against the fallen more tightly than Christ has shut it — drove him into schism, a rending of the body of Christ that no zeal for purity can justify. Reconciled, it is believed, before his death in exile as a confessor under persecution, he shows both that learning without lowliness may split the church, and that grace may yet recover a man from his own hard error.
webster_summary: A learned third-century writer of the Roman church whose rigorism drove him into schism as a rival bishop, reckoned the first antipope.
webster_full: HIPPOLYTUS OF ROME, proper noun. A Christian writer and presbyter of the Roman church in the early third century, about 170 to 235.
A man of great learning, author of commentaries on Daniel and the Song of Songs and of a refutation of heresies.
A rigorist who, contending against what he judged laxity toward penitents, went into schism and set up as a rival bishop.
Reckoned by later reckoning the first of the antipopes, for his separation from the lawful communion of the church.
Believed reconciled before his death in exile, dying a confessor under persecution.
scriptures: Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Rom 14:4
Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
corruption_summary: A learned man whose rigorism and schism must be named plainly as error, though his learning is honourable.
corruption_paragraphs: Hippolytus’s learning and his contendings for sound doctrine are honourable, and the church has been the richer for his writings. But his rigorism was error, not merely a stricter temper: he would have barred the door of restoration against grievous sinners whom the church, following her Lord, receives upon repentance; and by this severity he made himself the judge of another man’s servant, Romans 14:4, setting his own standard above the mercy of Christ who came to save that which was lost.

Worse, his rigorism ripened into schism. To rend the body of Christ, to set up altar against altar and bishop against bishop, is a corruption that no zeal for purity can sanctify, for the Lord commands us to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, Ephesians 4:3. That he is reckoned the first antipope is a mark of his fall, not his honour. We give thanks that grace, it is believed, recovered him to the communion of the church before his martyrdom, and we take his story as warning that learning without lowliness, and zeal without love, will split the very church they mean to purify.
roots_summary: That zeal for purity must never become the schism and rigorism that rend the body of Christ.
roots_lines: Learning and contending for sound doctrine are honourable, and the church is enriched by faithful writers.
Rigorism that shuts the door of restoration tighter than Christ has shut it is error, not superior holiness.
To judge another man’s servant and set up a rival altar is schism, and schism rends the body of Christ.
The unity of the Spirit is to be kept in the bond of peace, and no zeal justifies its breach.
Grace may yet recover a man from his own hard error, as it is believed to have recovered Hippolytus before his death.
usage: Hippolytus’s writings against heresy are honourable, yet his rigorism drove him into schism.
Reckoned the first antipope, Hippolytus is a warning that zeal without lowliness can split the church.
His story teaches that the door of restoration must not be shut tighter than Christ Himself has shut it.

etymology: From the Greek Methōdios, from methōdos, “a following after, a pursuit, a method” (from metá, after, and hodós, way). He is styled “of Olympus” from the Lycian see he is traditionally held to have governed, dying a martyr about 311.
biblical_def: Methodius of Olympus was an early bishop and confessor of the church, remembered chiefly as one of the first to contend openly against certain errors of Origen, that learned and influential teacher whose speculations upon the pre-existence of souls and the shape of the resurrection body strayed from the plain testimony of Scripture. Where Origen tended to allegorize away the resurrection of the flesh and to entertain the pre-existence of the soul, Methodius laboured to hold the church to the sober hope of the bodily resurrection, that this same body, sown in corruption, shall be raised in incorruption, 1 Corinthians 15:42, and that the man who dies is the man who shall rise. His best-known work, the Symposium or Banquet of the Ten Virgins, sets forth in the form of a discourse the praise of purity and virginity, drawing upon the parable of the wise and foolish virgins to commend a watchful and holy chastity while awaiting the Bridegroom. Though not every judgment in his writings is to be followed, and though his high estimate of virginity must be weighed against the honour Scripture gives to marriage, his stand for the resurrection of the body against speculative error, and his death as a martyr under Diocletian’s persecution, mark him as a faithful witness whose labour helped to guard the church’s hope.
webster_summary: An early bishop and martyr who opposed the errors of Origen and defended the bodily resurrection, author of the Symposium.
webster_full: METHODIUS OF OLYMPUS, proper noun. An early Christian bishop, traditionally of Olympus in Lycia, and a martyr about 311.
One of the first to contend openly against the speculative errors of Origen touching pre-existence and the resurrection.
A defender of the resurrection of the flesh, that this same body shall be raised incorruptible.
Author of the Symposium, or Banquet of the Ten Virgins, a discourse in praise of purity drawn from the parable of the virgins.
A confessor who sealed his testimony in martyrdom under the Diocletian persecution.
scriptures: So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption.
And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God.
Mat 25:1
Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom.
Dan 12:3
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness against speculative error, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the church’s hope of the bodily resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: Methodius’s labour was itself a defence of the truth against the errors of his age, for he stood against Origen’s speculations touching the pre-existence of souls and the dissolving of the resurrection body into allegory, holding fast instead to the plain apostolic hope that this same flesh, sown in corruption, shall be raised in incorruption, 1 Corinthians 15:42.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover through his life is the sober, literal hope of the resurrection of the body, which the church confesses against every philosophy that would spiritualize it away, and the watchfulness of the wise virgins who keep their lamps trimmed against the coming of the Bridegroom. That a man of the early church saw clearly enough to correct so towering a teacher as Origen reminds us that faithfulness to Scripture, not the reputation of a name, is the measure of truth, and that the resurrection of the flesh is no myth but the settled promise of God.
roots_summary: That the same body which dies shall be raised, and that faithfulness corrects even the most celebrated teacher.
roots_lines: This same body, sown in corruption, shall be raised in incorruption; the resurrection of the flesh is no allegory.
Speculation touching the pre-existence of souls strays from the plain testimony of Scripture and is rightly opposed.
The wise virgins keep their lamps trimmed, watching for the coming of the Bridegroom.
Faithfulness to the Word, not the fame of a teacher, is the measure of truth in the church.
A confessor’s martyrdom seals his testimony to the hope that is in Christ.
usage: Methodius opposed Origen’s errors and held the church to the hope of the bodily resurrection.
In the Symposium, Methodius drew from the parable of the ten virgins to commend a watchful purity.
His martyrdom under Diocletian sealed his witness to the resurrection of the flesh.

etymology: From the Latin Lactantius, a Roman family name perhaps connected with lactans, “giving milk, nourishing.” His full name was Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius; he flourished about 250 to 325 and was surnamed by later ages “the Christian Cicero” for the elegance of his Latin prose.
biblical_def: Lactantius was a Christian teacher of rhetoric in the age of the last great persecution and the dawn of Constantine’s peace, a man so polished in his Latin that later ages named him “the Christian Cicero.” Converted from paganism, he turned the eloquence he had once employed in the schools of the empire to the defence of the faith, setting forth in his great work, the Divine Institutes, a reasoned overthrow of the folly of idolatry and the wisdom of the philosophers, and a commendation of the true God and of the righteousness that comes by Him. He wrote also of the deaths of the persecutors, recounting how the LORD requited those emperors who had lifted their hands against His church, a solemn testimony that the God who is not mocked will render to every man according to his deeds. So esteemed was his learning that the emperor Constantine appointed him tutor to his son Crispus. Not every point of his doctrine is to be received without weighing, for his early training left traces of imperfection in his grasp of the deep things of God, and he wrote before the great creeds had refined the church’s speech; yet his labour to show that the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God, 1 Corinthians 3:19, and to commend the gospel to a learned and pagan age, marks him a faithful and useful witness whose eloquence was laid at the feet of Christ.
webster_summary: A Christian rhetorician surnamed the Christian Cicero, author of the Divine Institutes and tutor to Constantine’s son.
webster_full: LACTANTIUS, proper noun. A Christian teacher of rhetoric flourishing about 250 to 325, in the age of Diocletian and Constantine.
Surnamed the Christian Cicero for the elegance of his Latin prose, converted from paganism to the faith.
Author of the Divine Institutes, a reasoned defence of the true God against idolatry and pagan philosophy.
Author also of a treatise on the deaths of the persecutors, recounting God’s judgment upon the enemies of His church.
Appointed by the emperor Constantine to be tutor to his son Crispus.
scriptures: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
Psa 14:1
The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
corruption_summary: A faithful and eloquent apologist, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle that all learning must serve the truth of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Lactantius took the eloquence he had learned in the pagan schools and consecrated it wholly to the defence of the faith, overthrowing the folly of idolatry and setting the true God before a learned and unbelieving age — a labour that shows how the church may plunder the treasures of the world’s learning and lay them at the feet of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle his life recovers is that all human learning, eloquence, and philosophy find their right use only in the service of the truth of God, and that the wisdom of this world, however polished, is foolishness with Him when it is set against His gospel. Though Lactantius wrote before the creeds had refined the church’s speech, and not every judgment of his is to be followed, his consecrated eloquence remains a pattern: gifts of mind are not to be despised but to be baptized into the service of Christ, that the wise of the world may be taken in their own craftiness and brought to bow before the wisdom of God.
roots_summary: That the learning and eloquence of the world are rightly used only when laid at the feet of Christ.
roots_lines: The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God when it is set against His gospel.
Gifts of eloquence and learning are not to be despised, but consecrated to the defence of the truth.
God is not mocked; He requites the persecutors who lift their hands against His church.
The church may plunder the treasures of pagan learning and lay them at the feet of Christ.
A man converted from the schools of the empire may become a faithful witness to the true God.
usage: Lactantius, the Christian Cicero, laid his pagan eloquence at the feet of Christ in the Divine Institutes.
His treatise on the deaths of the persecutors testifies that God is not mocked.
Constantine esteemed his learning enough to make him tutor to his son Crispus.

etymology: From the Greek Theodōretos, “given by God” (from Theos, God, and dōretos, given as a gift), a name akin to Theodore and Dorothea. He is styled “of Cyrus” from the small Syrian see he shepherded (c. 393–458).
biblical_def: Theodoret of Cyrus was a bishop of the Antiochene school, an able and industrious expositor of Scripture and a historian of the church, who governed a small and rustic Syrian diocese with pastoral care while pouring out a stream of learned writings. Trained in the Antiochene manner, which prized the plain, historical, and grammatical sense of the text against wild allegory, he wrote commentaries upon the Psalms and the prophets and the epistles of Paul that remain valued for their sobriety and their attention to what the words actually say — a discipline the Reformers would afterward prize, that the Scripture is to be interpreted according to its true and natural sense, not spiritualized at the interpreter’s whim. He wrote also an Ecclesiastical History continuing the record of the church’s trials and triumphs, and a defence of the faith against the errors of the heathen. He was caught up in the fierce Christological contentions of his age, standing at times against Cyril and being embroiled in the controversies that led to Chalcedon, where at length he confessed the orthodox faith and was restored. Not every position he took in those struggles is to be commended, and his sympathies with certain Antiochene teachers drew suspicion; yet his labour as a careful expositor who honoured the plain sense of the Word, and his final confession of the truth, mark him a servant whose diligence in the Scriptures the church may still profit from.
webster_summary: A fifth-century Antiochene bishop, exegete, and church historian who prized the plain sense of Scripture, valued for his sober commentaries.
webster_full: THEODORET OF CYRUS, proper noun. A bishop of the Syrian see of Cyrus, about 393 to 458, of the Antiochene school.
An industrious expositor of Scripture, commenting on the Psalms, the prophets, and the epistles of Paul in the plain, historical sense.
A church historian, author of an Ecclesiastical History continuing the record of the church’s trials.
A defender of the faith against heathen error and a participant in the Christological controversies leading to Chalcedon.
One who at length confessed the orthodox faith and was restored to the church’s communion.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: A careful expositor, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of interpreting Scripture in its plain and natural sense.
corruption_paragraphs: Theodoret’s enduring worth lies in his sober handling of the sacred text, for the Antiochene discipline he practised — giving the sense, causing the people to understand the reading, Nehemiah 8:8 — against wild and arbitrary allegory anticipated the Reformers’ own insistence that Scripture has one true and natural sense, to be sought by grammar and context and not conjured at the interpreter’s pleasure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle his life recovers is the right dividing of the word of truth, 2 Timothy 2:15, that the expositor is a workman answerable to God for handling the text faithfully according to what it says. Though he was entangled in the bitter controversies of his age and not every judgment of his is to be followed, and though he at first resisted where he ought to have submitted, his diligence in the Scriptures and his final confession of the orthodox faith commend him as a labourer from whose care in the Word the church may still learn.
roots_summary: That Scripture is to be rightly divided according to its plain and natural sense, as a workman answerable to God.
roots_lines: The Scripture has one true and natural sense, to be sought by grammar and context, not conjured by allegory.
The faithful expositor gives the sense and causes the people to understand the reading.
The workman must rightly divide the word of truth, answerable to God for how he handles the text.
Diligence in searching the Scriptures daily is the noble mark of the Bereans and of every faithful teacher.
A man entangled in controversy may yet, confessing the truth at last, be restored to the church.
usage: Theodoret’s Antiochene commentaries are valued for honouring the plain sense of the text.
His Ecclesiastical History continued the record of the church’s trials into the fifth century.
Embroiled in the controversies of Chalcedon, Theodoret at last confessed the orthodox faith.

etymology: From the Latin Tertius, “the third,” a common Roman name given, like Secundus and Quartus, according to birth-order in a household. He appears once, as the amanuensis who wrote the Epistle to the Romans at Paul’s dictation, greeting the church in his own hand, Romans 16:22.
biblical_def: Tertius is a name we should never have known but for a single sentence, in which he steps for a moment from behind the apostle’s dictation to add his own greeting: “I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord,” Romans 16:22. He was the amanuensis, the penman, to whom the apostle Paul dictated the great Epistle to the Romans — that towering exposition of justification by faith, of the ruin of man and the righteousness of God, of election and of the mercies by which we present our bodies a living sacrifice. The mighty words were the apostle’s, given by the Holy Ghost; the hand that formed the letters upon the parchment was the hand of Tertius. There is a lowly and blessed dignity in this hidden labour, that a man should be found faithful in the office of a scribe, 1 Corinthians 4:2, employed not to compose but to write, not to be seen but to serve, and yet be caught up into the greatest of the epistles. He salutes the church “in the Lord,” and so we know him for a brother, a believing man doing believing work. The Lord who sees in secret has recorded the name of His scribe, and thereby honoured every quiet servant whose faithful hand advances a work greater than himself.
webster_summary: The amanuensis who wrote the Epistle to the Romans at Paul’s dictation, greeting the church in his own name in Romans 16:22.
webster_full: TERTIUS, proper noun. A Christian brother named once in Scripture, the penman of the Epistle to the Romans.
The amanuensis to whom the apostle Paul dictated the letter, forming its words upon the parchment.
One who adds his own greeting to the church, saluting them in the Lord, Romans 16:22.
A pattern of the lowly and faithful servant employed in a work greater than himself.
A believing man, known to us only by his hidden labour and his greeting in the Lord.
scriptures: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
corruption_summary: A faithful servant, not a contested doctrine; his hidden labour recovers the dignity of quiet, faithful work done unto the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Tertius has no history apart from his one greeting, and there is nothing in his name for the world to redefine, for he is simply a believing man who wrote what a greater man dictated, and did it in the Lord.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle his brief mention recovers is the dignity of hidden and faithful labour, that it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful, 1 Corinthians 4:2, and that the humblest office — a scribe’s hand, a penman’s patience — is honoured of God when it is done heartily as unto the Lord and not unto men. The world prizes the author and forgets the scribe; but the Lord who sees in secret recorded the name of Tertius in the very epistle he penned, teaching every quiet servant that no faithful work is unseen by Him, and that the good and faithful servant, faithful over a few things, shall enter into the joy of his Lord.
roots_summary: That the hidden and faithful labourer, though the world forget him, is remembered and honoured of God.
roots_lines: The mighty words of Romans were the apostle’s by the Spirit; the faithful hand that wrote them was the scribe’s.
It is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful, whether in great office or in lowly.
Whatsoever we do is to be done heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
The Lord who sees in secret records the name of His quiet servant, that no faithful work is unseen.
The good and faithful servant, faithful over a few things, shall enter into the joy of his Lord.
usage: Tertius, the penman of Romans, greets the church in his own hand in Romans 16:22.
The apostle dictated and Tertius wrote, a pattern of the hidden servant honoured of God.
That Scripture records the name of the scribe teaches the dignity of quiet, faithful labour.

etymology: From the Greek Narkissos, the name of a flower and, in Greek legend, of a youth, thought to be connected with nárke, “numbness, torpor.” It was borne by a Roman householder whose people in the Lord are greeted by the apostle Paul in Romans 16:11.
biblical_def: Narcissus is known to us solely through a single greeting, in which the apostle Paul salutes “them which are of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord,” Romans 16:11. The words are carefully chosen, for the apostle does not necessarily greet Narcissus himself, but those of his household who are in the Lord — the believing servants and members of a great man’s house at Rome. Here is a precious thing: that within the establishment of a wealthy or notable Roman, whose own standing before God is not affirmed, there was a company of the redeemed, slaves it may be, and dependents, who had been called out of darkness into the marvellous light of Christ and gathered into His church. The gospel had entered under that roof and claimed its own, not the master perhaps, but the servants; not the great, but the lowly whom God delights to choose, 1 Corinthians 1:26. That Paul knew them, named them, and joined them to the fellowship of the saints at Rome shows the care of Christ for the least and most obscure of His people. The household of Narcissus reminds us that grace runs where it will, plucking believers even from the houses of the powerful, and that the true company of the faithful is often the hidden remnant “in the Lord” within a house that does not own His name.
webster_summary: A Roman householder whose members in the Lord are greeted by Paul in Romans 16:11.
webster_full: NARCISSUS, proper noun. A man at Rome named once in Scripture, in the greetings of the sixteenth chapter of Romans.
The head of a household within which were believers, saluted by the apostle Paul.
Not himself necessarily greeted, but “them which are of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord.”
A witness that the gospel gathered its own even within the houses of the notable at Rome.
A name that marks the hidden company of the faithful within a great man’s establishment.
scriptures: Salute them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord.
For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.
Phi 4:22
All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light.
corruption_summary: A hidden company of believers, not a contested doctrine; the household of Narcissus recovers the reach of grace into the houses of the great.
corruption_paragraphs: Narcissus is a name upon which nothing rests but a single greeting, and there is nothing in it for the age to redefine; he is simply the head of a Roman house within which the gospel had found and claimed a believing company.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle this brief mention recovers is the free and searching reach of sovereign grace, which calls not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble, 1 Corinthians 1:26, but plucks its own even from the households of the powerful — servants and dependents made a chosen generation, called out of darkness into His marvellous light. As Paul could greet the saints of Caesar’s own household, Philippians 4:22, so he greets the believers under the roof of Narcissus, teaching us that the true church is often a hidden remnant “in the Lord” within a house that does not own His name, and that no establishment, however great, is beyond the entrance of the gospel.
roots_summary: That sovereign grace reaches into the houses of the great, calling a hidden remnant to be the Lord’s own.
roots_lines: The apostle greets not the master but those of the household who are in the Lord, the believing remnant within.
God calls not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble, but chooses the lowly to His praise.
Grace runs where it will, gathering its own even from the households of the powerful at Rome.
As saints were found in Caesar’s household, so believers were found under the roof of Narcissus.
The true church is often the hidden company “in the Lord” within a house that does not own His name.
usage: Paul greets those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord, Romans 16:11.
The household of Narcissus shows grace claiming a remnant within a great Roman house.
That believers were found under such a roof recovers the searching reach of sovereign grace.

etymology: From the Latin Julia, the feminine of Julius, the name of a great Roman clan (the gens Julia); a common name among Roman women, and often borne by freedwomen of that house. She is greeted once as a saint at Rome in Romans 16:15.
biblical_def: Julia is one of the many saints whom the apostle Paul salutes by name in the roll of greetings closing his Epistle to the Romans: “Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them,” Romans 16:15. She is named, it appears, with Philologus, perhaps his wife or a kinswoman, among a little company of believers gathered together, one of that great host of ordinary saints whose faith the apostle knew and whom he loved in Christ. Of her deeds and her history Scripture tells us nothing further; she is simply a believing woman, a member of the body of Christ at Rome, remembered by the Holy Ghost in the sacred record. And this is her honour, that the Spirit of God should set down her name among the saints, for it is a great and blessed thing to be known and named of God, to have one’s name written in the Lamb’s book of life, Revelation 21:27, and to be numbered among that holy company whom the apostle greets as beloved. Julia teaches us that the church is made up not chiefly of the famous but of the faithful, ordinary believers whose names the world forgets but whom God remembers, and that to be a saint in Christ, known and greeted in the Lord, is a dignity beyond all the honours of the world.
webster_summary: A believing woman greeted by Paul as a saint at Rome in Romans 16:15.
webster_full: JULIA, proper noun. A Christian woman at Rome named once in Scripture, in the greetings closing the Epistle to the Romans.
Saluted by the apostle Paul among Philologus, Nereus, Olympas, and the saints with them.
Named perhaps with Philologus as wife or kinswoman, a member of a little company of believers.
One of the great host of ordinary saints whose faith the apostle knew and loved in Christ.
A believing woman whose name the Holy Ghost has set down in the sacred record.
scriptures: Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them.

Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
corruption_summary: A faithful saint, not a contested doctrine; her name recovers the honour of the ordinary believer whom God remembers.
corruption_paragraphs: Julia is a name upon which nothing rests but a single greeting, and there is nothing in it for the present age to redefine; she is simply a believing woman, a saint at Rome, greeted and loved by the apostle in the Lord.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle her name recovers is the honour of the ordinary, faithful believer whom the world forgets but whom God remembers, for the Lord keeps a book of remembrance for them that fear Him and think upon His name, Malachi 3:16. It is a greater thing that her name is written in heaven, Luke 10:20, and in the Lamb’s book of life, than that it should be famous upon earth. Julia teaches us that the church is built not of the celebrated but of the faithful, that to be known and named of God as a saint in Christ is a dignity beyond every honour the world can give, and that no believer, however obscure, is forgotten by the God who has written her name in His book.
roots_summary: That the ordinary, faithful believer, forgotten by the world, is known and remembered by God.
roots_lines: The Spirit of God set down the name of Julia among the saints, honouring an obscure and faithful woman.

usage: Paul salutes Julia among the saints at Rome in Romans 16:15.
Julia’s name, set down by the Spirit, honours the ordinary faithful believer.
That her name is written in heaven is a greater honour than any fame upon earth.

etymology: From the Hebrew Choglāh, thought to mean “partridge” or perhaps “dance, whirl.” She was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh, who received an inheritance in the land of promise, Numbers 27 and 36.
biblical_def: Hoglah was the third named of the five daughters of Zelophehad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — of the tribe of Manasseh, whose father died in the wilderness having no sons. In an age when inheritance passed from father to son, these sisters came before Moses, and before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation at the door of the tabernacle, pleading that their father’s name should not be done away from among his family for want of a son, and asking a possession among the brethren of their father, Numbers 27:4. Moses brought their cause before the LORD, and the LORD Himself vindicated it, saying, “The daughters of Zelophehad speak right,” and commanding that they be given an inheritance, and establishing thereby a statute of judgment in Israel. Later, in Numbers 36, the tribe raised the question lest their inheritance, by marriage outside the tribe, pass to another; and the LORD provided that they should marry within their father’s tribe, that no inheritance remove from tribe to tribe. So Hoglah and her sisters took their portion in the land, married into the families of Manasseh, and kept their father’s name alive in his inheritance. In these godly women we see faith that laid hold upon the promise of the land, a reverent boldness that sought its cause in the right way before the LORD, and a providence that wrote their names forever in the sacred record.
webster_summary: One of the five daughters of Zelophehad who received an inheritance in the land, her cause vindicated by the LORD in Numbers 27 and 36.
webster_full: HOGLAH, proper noun. The third named of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh.
One of five sisters whose father died in the wilderness leaving no sons.
A woman who, with her sisters, sought and received an inheritance in the land of promise.
One whose cause the LORD Himself vindicated, saying, “The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.”
One who married within her father’s tribe that the inheritance should not remove from tribe to tribe.

corruption_summary: A faithful daughter of Israel, not a contested doctrine; her inheritance recovers the LORD’s care for the fatherless and the keeping of a father’s name.
corruption_paragraphs: Hoglah’s story is a plain and honourable one, of faith laying hold upon the promise of the land in the right way, and it needs no reshaping to serve any cause; the LORD Himself pronounced that she and her sisters spoke right, and settled their inheritance by His own word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle her account recovers is the tender justice of the LORD toward the fatherless and the daughter without a brother, and the keeping alive of a father’s name and portion in Israel, so that a goodly heritage was given her and the lines fell to her in pleasant places, Psalm 16:6. Here is no manifesto but a testimony to providence, that the God who orders inheritances remembered five sisters by name and wrote them forever in His book; and to faith, that they sought their cause reverently before the LORD and received from His hand a possession in the land of promise, a foretaste of that better inheritance, incorruptible and undefiled, reserved in heaven for all His children.
roots_summary: That the LORD is tender toward the fatherless and keeps alive the name and inheritance of His people.
roots_lines: The daughters of Zelophehad sought their inheritance reverently before the LORD, and He said they spake right.
The LORD is the God of the fatherless, who kept a father’s name and portion alive through his daughters.

Faith lays hold upon the promise of the land, seeking its cause in the right way and not by force.

etymology: From the Hebrew Milkāh, “queen” or “counsel,” akin to melek, king. Here it is the name of the fourth of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh, who received an inheritance in the land, Numbers 27 and 36 — to be distinguished from the earlier Milcah, wife of Nahor.
biblical_def: Milcah was the fourth named of the five daughters of Zelophehad — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah — of the tribe of Manasseh, sisters left without a brother when their father died in the wilderness. Together they came before Moses and Eleazar and the congregation at the door of the tabernacle, pleading that their father’s name might not perish from his family, and seeking a possession among the brethren of their father, Numbers 27:4. Their request was no rebellion against the order the LORD had set, but a reverent laying hold upon the promise of the inheritance in Canaan, made in the right way and in due order; and the LORD honoured it, declaring through Moses that they spoke right and that an inheritance should surely be given them. So this became a settled statute of judgment in Israel, that where a man died without a son his inheritance should pass to his daughter. When afterward the heads of Manasseh feared the loss of that portion by marriage outside the tribe, the LORD provided that these daughters should marry within their father’s tribe, and so Milcah took her portion and kept it within Manasseh. She stands, with her sisters, as a witness that the LORD remembers the daughter as well as the son, that He orders every inheritance by His wise providence, and that faith which seeks its cause reverently before Him shall not be put to shame.
webster_summary: One of the five daughters of Zelophehad who received an inheritance in the land, distinct from the earlier Milcah, wife of Nahor.
webster_full: MILCAH, proper noun. The fourth named of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh.
One of five sisters left without a brother when their father died in the wilderness.
A woman who, with her sisters, sought and received a possession in the land of promise.
One whose inheritance the LORD confirmed as a statute of judgment in Israel.
To be distinguished from the earlier Milcah, the wife of Nahor and grandmother of Rebekah.

The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
corruption_summary: A faithful daughter of Israel, not a contested doctrine; her inheritance recovers the LORD’s remembering of the daughter and His ordering of every portion.
corruption_paragraphs: Milcah’s story is a plain testimony of faith and obedience, that she and her sisters sought their inheritance reverently and in due order, and did even as the LORD commanded Moses, Numbers 36:10; it is not raw material for any modern cause but a record of godly women who honoured the LORD in seeking His promise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle her account recovers is that the LORD remembers the daughter as surely as the son, ordering every inheritance by His own wise and gracious providence, and that a goodly heritage falls to His people because the lines are cast by His hand, Psalm 16:6. Milcah’s portion was not seized but received, sought in the right way and granted by the word of the LORD, and kept within her father’s tribe according to His command — a pattern of that submissive, believing obedience by which the saints receive from God what He has promised, and a pledge of the incorruptible inheritance reserved in heaven for all who are His.
roots_summary: That the LORD remembers the daughter, orders every inheritance by His providence, and honours believing obedience.
